Authors:[Ricard Solé](https://arxiv.org/search/physics?searchtype=author&query=Sol%C3%A9,+R), [Giulio Ruffini](https://arxiv.org/search/physics?searchtype=author&query=Ruffini,+G), [Francesca Castaldo](https://arxiv.org/search/physics?searchtype=author&query=Castaldo,+F), [Marco Tuccio](https://arxiv.org/search/physics?searchtype=author&query=Tuccio,+M), [Luis F. View a PDF of the paper titled Large-Language Models as a Cognitive Virus, by Ricard Sol\'e and 8 other authors

[View PDF](/pdf/2609.03344)
[HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.03344v1)
> Abstract:Large-language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming part of human culture, reshaping how information is produced, transmitted, and used. Here we propose that their diffusion can be understood through a viral analogy, with LLM use spreading through populations, becoming embedded in cognitive and cultural practices. We model transitions among uncoupled, coupled, and persistently dependent users, and show that the interplay between social transmission, recovery, and collective reinforcement can generate tipping points and technological lock-in. A central consequence is the possibility of runaway dynamics: once a critical threshold is crossed, small increases in adoption can trigger rapid population-level shifts toward persistent dependence, with abrupt losses in cognitive competence. The same framework, however, identifies conditions for cognitive immunization, based on reducing transmission and facilitating reversibility. Our results highlight how LLM adoption may involve nonlinear collective transitions with important consequences for cognitive autonomy.

중간 연산은 단계 객체(스테이트레스 오퍼레이션)를 생성해 등록만 하고, 실행 로직은 내부 싱크 체인에 위임되어 즉시 수행되지 않는다
findFirst와 같은 터미널 연산이 호출되면 요소가 순차적으로 파이프라인을 통과하고, 첫 매칭 요소가 결정되면 이후 요소는 전혀 처리되지 않는다

이벤트 기반 시스템에서 싱크 체인 조립 방식을 차용해 이벤트 핸들러를 싱크로 변환하고, 구독(터미널) 시점에만 실제 이벤트 전파를 수행한다

quiz.question: 왜 filter와 map 같은 중간 연산은 터미널 연산이 호출될 때까지 실행되지 않는가?
quiz.explanation: 중간 연산은 스트림을 반환하면서 단계만 등록하고, 실제 데이터 처리 로직은 터미널 연산이 호출될 때 비로소 실행된다

quiz.question: findFirst 터미널 연산이 매칭 요소를 찾았을 때 발생하는 흐름은?
quiz.explanation: findFirst는 첫 매칭 요소가 확정되면 즉시 파이프라인 실행을 중단하고, 남은 요소는 평가되지 않는다

raw.body:
# There's No Limit to How Bad Code Can Get

- 04 September 2026
- [software-engineering](/tags/software-engineering/),
- [essay](/tags/essay/)

TL;DR: Metaphors like "a sinking ship" are often used to describe codebases, but are misleading.
A *business* will sink long before code quality reaches a hypothetical floor. Technical debt has
no bankruptcy, no clean reset, so metaphors that imply an end provide a false sense of security.

> [Software is in the domain of the abstract. It is not like a building, or a bridge, that is in
> the physical realm where you can see and feel the nature of the thing. If you continue to add
> floors and rooms to a building forever, it will collapse. Software faces no such constraint.
> The code can **always** get worse. There can **always** be a new layer of indirection
> or a reduction in performance.](#pull-quote-source)

## 1: Boarding a sinking ship

Over a decade ago I had my first encounter with an *ugly* legacy codebase. I had just joined Amazon
as a "Software Development Engineer", fresh out of university, and worked on a team that owned code
related to [processing orders](#1-note). On the surface, what our code had to
do seemed simple. Processing an order involved writing some things to a database and calling into
services owned by other teams, either to ask validity questions or to update bookkeeping on their
end. My colleagues and I estimated that a sufficient implementation of this system shouldn't need
more than two dozen strong engineers to maintain and evolve. Yet, our organization was
hundreds of people, and the system had grown so large and complex that it had become impossible to
learn how it all worked.

It was rare to stay longer than a few years in this org, and institutional knowledge had eroded. This
resulted in code that was full of ["haunted graveyards"](#2-note). Fear suppressed any (under-rewarded) efforts to
simplify existing systems. The business rules for what had to be done for each type of order were
decided by people long ago who weren't around anymore. These rules could sometimes be found in a
hopelessly out of date file proudly calling itself a 'living document', but often the rules simply
were not written anywhere we could find. Tracing behavior yourself wasn't easy either because much
of the system lived across team boundaries where the code was not easy to access.

When some obscure process wasn't happening with an order that should have been happening, our pagers
would angrily notify us that someone in our tangled web of service dependencies was unhappy. As a
result of this feedback mechanism, the system stayed afloat, but remained difficult to change
and had [abysmal performance](#3-note). Despite this, new layers were constantly added to support the latest
Amazon products and features. This felt unsustainable, and this feeling is what makes me and others
reach for a "sinking ship" as a metaphor to describe an organization that doesn't pay down their
technical debt.

To their credit, there were always [ongoing attempts](#4-note) to fix the architecture, and these usually
went as follows: A new manager or senior engineer joins the organization and observes that "things are bad".
Leadership at the organization agrees and *wants* to make things better, but there are no engineers
available, so each fix attempt includes adding new engineers and [teams](#5-note).

The re-architectures were always a failure: The system required *years* of study to properly
understand and was constantly changing. It's not politically viable to take so long to design a
fix for the system, so naturally everyone attempting to fix things must work with
incomplete information. Some of this impatience is from within: If you are trying to
design a grand fix for such a prominently painful architecture, you are doing it in part because
you want a promotion (and you don't want to wait too long for a promotion).

Each cycle would end with the remains of the new attempt permanently grafted onto our architecture
and the leading engineer having departed with their requisite promotion. The increased headcount
stays because the migration plans are too painful and unpopular to actually finish. [The cycle
continued](#6-note) as it had long before I had arrived. The sinking ship seemed to have no end.

## 2: Where *does* it end?

About three years after I had left, I was chatting on the phone with a former colleague from that
team. He had recently left the company after an impressive 6-year tenure and had witnessed the
cycle complete again. We were commiserating, and both of us reached for the sinking ship metaphor
to describe the org, despite us having left years apart.

"Where does it end? How does it end?" he asked me, curious to hear my take on what would happen to
that org in the future.

The question and metaphor didn't sit right with me, and I realized the question conflated two
things. Are we talking about the code, or are we talking about the company?

key_points.point: 기술 부채는 파산 개념이 없으며 코드 품질은 물리적 한계 없이 계속 악화될 수 있다
‘침몰하는 배’ 비유는 비즈니스가 코드보다 먼저 실패한다는 사실을 가려 위험한 오해를 만든다
불완전한 정보와 정치·인센티브 문제 때문에 대규모 재구축 시도가 반복적으로 실패한다

production_ideas: 서비스 의존성 알림(pager) 방식을 데이터 파이프라인 지연 알림으로 옮겨 실시간 성능 감시를 강화한다
기술 부채 전용 스프린트를 도입해 작은 리팩터링을 지속적으로 수행함으로써 대규모 재구축 위험을 감소시킨다
비즈니스 규칙을 버전 관리된 설정 파일에 기록해 조직 내 지식 손실을 방지하고 변경 시 검증 절차를 자동화한다

options: 물리적 구조와 달리 소프트웨어는 파산 개념이 없기 때문이다
코드는 언제든지 성능이 향상될 수 있다
quiz.explanation: 본문은 기술 부채는 파산이 없으며, 코드가 무한히 악화될 수 있다고 강조해 비유가 오해를 낳는다고 설명한다.

quiz.question: 조직이 레거시 시스템을 재구성하려 할 때 가장 큰 실패 원인은?
options: 충분한 엔지니어가 없어서 새로운 팀을 늘린다
시스템 이해에 수년이 필요해 설계가 지연된다
quiz.explanation: 본문은 시스템을 제대로 이해하려면 수년이 걸리며, 그 기간 동안 설계가 불완전해져 재구축이 실패한다고 지적한다.
